questions.question: What does EBS stand for?

explanation.correct: EBS stands for Elastic Block Storage — a network-attached block storage service for EC2.
explanation.why: Elastic Beanstalk (not Beanstack) is a compute/PaaS service, not storage.

questions.question: How is EBS storage attached to an EC2 instance?

options.text: Physically, directly on the host machine

explanation.correct: EBS is a network-attached storage service — the disk lives on a separate device connected via AWS's internal network.
explanation.why: Instance Store (not EBS) is the physically attached disk on the host machine.

questions.question: Which storage type is directly attached to the physical host machine running your EC2 instance?

explanation.correct: Instance Store is a physical disk directly attached to the host machine — it is ephemeral (temporary).
explanation.why: EBS is network-attached. EFS and S3 are separate services entirely.

questions.question: What happens to Instance Store data when an EC2 instance is stopped or terminated?

options.text: Data is backed up to S3

explanation.correct: Instance Store is ephemeral — data is permanently lost when the instance is stopped, terminated, or the host fails.
explanation.why: Unlike EBS, Instance Store has no persistence beyond the life of the running instance.

questions.question: Which EBS volume type is best for most general-purpose workloads?

explanation.correct: gp2 (General Purpose SSD) and gp3 (newer generation) balance price and performance for most workloads.
explanation.why: io1 is for high-performance databases. st1/sc1 are HDDs for throughput and infrequent access.

questions.question: Which EBS volume type provides the highest IOPS for mission-critical applications?

explanation.correct: io1 (Provisioned IOPS SSD) delivers up to 64,000 IOPS per volume — designed for I/O-intensive databases.
explanation.why: gp2 maxes at 16,000 IOPS. st1 and sc1 are HDDs with much lower IOPS.

questions.question: What is the maximum IOPS per volume for gp2?

explanation.correct: gp2 supports up to 16,000 IOPS per volume.
explanation.why: 64,000 is io1's limit. 80,000 is the max per instance (applies across all attached volumes). 3,000 is gp3's baseline.

questions.question: What is the volume size range for io1 EBS volumes?

explanation.correct: io1 (Provisioned IOPS SSD) supports volumes from 4 GiB to 16 TiB.
explanation.why: gp2 starts at 1 GiB. st1 and sc1 start at 500 GiB. EBS Magnetic (legacy) maxes at 1 TiB.

questions.question: Which EBS volume type is ideal for Big Data and Data Warehouses?

explanation.correct: st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) is designed for frequently accessed, throughput-intensive workloads like Big Data and data warehouses.
explanation.why: gp2/io1 are SSDs for IOPS-sensitive tasks. sc1 is for less-frequently accessed cold data.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of EBS over Instance Store?

options.text: Data persists independently of the EC2 instance lifecycle

explanation.correct: EBS data persists even if the EC2 instance is stopped, rebooted, or terminated — it is independent of the instance lifecycle.
explanation.why: Instance Store data is lost on stop/terminate. EBS is not always faster or cheaper.

questions.question: Can an EBS volume exist without being attached to an EC2 instance?

options.text: No, it must always be attached
Yes, but AWS charges for the unattached volume
Yes, and AWS does not charge for unattached volumes

explanation.correct: EBS volumes can exist independently. AWS charges for provisioned storage regardless of whether it is attached to an instance.
explanation.why: Unattached EBS volumes still incur storage costs — you must delete them manually to stop charges.

questions.question: Which command lists all block devices (disks and partitions) on a Linux EC2 instance?

explanation.correct: lsblk lists all block devices including their names, sizes, and mount points — the first step when attaching a new EBS volume.
explanation.why: df -h shows disk usage of mounted filesystems only. lsblk shows all devices including unmounted ones.

questions.question: What must you do FIRST after attaching a brand-new EBS volume to a running EC2 instance?

options.text: Format it with a filesystem (e.g., XFS or ext4), then mount it
Nothing — it is ready to use immediately

explanation.correct: A new EBS volume is raw storage. You must format it (mkfs.xfs or mkfs.ext4) and then mount it before Linux can use it.
explanation.why: Only root volumes (boot) come pre-formatted. Additional volumes are blank and must be initialized.

questions.question: What is the difference between scale-up (vertical scaling) and scale-out (horizontal scaling) for EBS?

options.text: Scale-up adds more instances; scale-out increases volume size
Scale-up increases the size of an existing volume; scale-out attaches additional volumes
Scale-up is only for Instance Store

explanation.correct: Vertical scaling (scale-up) increases an existing EBS volume's size. Horizontal scaling (scale-out) attaches additional EBS volumes to the instance.
explanation.why: These are distinct approaches to growing storage capacity in AWS.

questions.question: After resizing an EBS volume in the AWS console, what additional step is required on the EC2 instance?

options.text: Grow the filesystem using growpart and xfs_growfs (or resize2fs)
Nothing — the OS detects it automatically

explanation.correct: After expanding the EBS volume in the console, you must also expand the partition (growpart) and then grow the filesystem (xfs_growfs or resize2fs) to use the new space.
explanation.why: The OS does not automatically recognize the expanded storage — the filesystem must be explicitly extended.

questions.question: What is an EBS Snapshot?

options.text: A live copy of an EBS volume
A point-in-time backup of an EBS volume stored in S3
A read-only replica of an EBS volume in another AZ
An AMI image of an EC2 instance

explanation.correct: An EBS Snapshot is a point-in-time backup stored durably in Amazon S3. Snapshots are incremental — only changed blocks are saved after the first full backup.
explanation.why: Snapshots are stored in S3 (internally) but managed via the EC2 console, not the S3 console.

questions.question: EBS Snapshots are incremental. What does this mean?

options.text: Each snapshot is a full copy of the volume
Only the first snapshot is full; subsequent snapshots save only changed blocks
Snapshots are taken automatically every hour
Incremental means snapshots are stored in multiple AZs

explanation.correct: The first snapshot is a full copy. Each subsequent snapshot only captures blocks that changed since the last snapshot — saving time and storage cost.
explanation.why: This incremental design means restoring from any single snapshot still gives you the complete volume.

questions.question: You need to move an EBS volume from us-east-1a to us-east-1b (different Availability Zones). How?

options.text: Directly move it in the console
Take a snapshot, then create a new volume from the snapshot in us-east-1b
Detach and reattach in a different AZ

explanation.correct: EBS volumes are AZ-specific. To move across AZs, take a snapshot and create a new volume from it in the target AZ.
explanation.why: You can also copy snapshots across Regions using the same approach.

questions.question: What is the dominant performance attribute for st1 and sc1 EBS volume types?

explanation.correct: st1 and sc1 are HDD types optimized for throughput (MB/s) — not IOPS. gp2 and io1 are IOPS-dominant.
explanation.why: HDDs have lower IOPS but excel at sequential throughput — ideal for streaming large datasets.

questions.question: Which EBS volume type can you NOT use as a boot volume?

explanation.correct: st1 and sc1 (HDD types) cannot be used as boot volumes. Only SSD types (gp2, gp3, io1, io2) can boot an EC2 instance.
explanation.why: Boot volumes require random read performance that HDDs cannot provide efficiently.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about gp3 compared to gp2?

options.text: gp3 is older and less capable
gp3 performance is tied to volume size like gp2
gp3 allows independent configuration of IOPS and throughput from storage size
gp3 is more expensive than gp2

explanation.correct: gp3 decouples performance from storage size — you can configure IOPS (up to 16,000) and throughput (up to 1,000 MB/s) independently of the disk size.
explanation.why: gp2 ties IOPS to size (3 IOPS/GB). gp3 is ~20% cheaper and AWS recommends migrating from gp2 to gp3.

questions.question: What is the default filesystem used on Amazon Linux 2 instances?

explanation.correct: Amazon Linux 2 uses XFS as its default filesystem. ext4 is another common Linux filesystem but not the Amazon Linux default.
explanation.why: XFS is high-performance and handles large files well — well-suited for cloud storage workloads.

questions.question: What is the maximum IOPS per volume for io1?

explanation.correct: io1 supports up to 64,000 IOPS per volume — the highest of any EBS volume type.
explanation.why: 80,000 is the per-instance maximum across all attached volumes. gp2/gp3 max at 16,000 per volume.

questions.question: An EBS volume must be in the same _______ as the EC2 instance it is attached to.

explanation.correct: EBS volumes are scoped to a specific Availability Zone. The volume and the EC2 instance must be in the same AZ to attach.
explanation.why: This AZ constraint is why snapshots are used to migrate volumes across AZs or Regions.

questions.question: A company needs storage for a high-frequency trading application requiring 50,000 IOPS with sub-millisecond latency. Which EBS type is appropriate?

explanation.correct: io1 (Provisioned IOPS SSD) is designed for I/O-intensive workloads requiring consistent, high IOPS performance — ideal for mission-critical, latency-sensitive applications.
explanation.why: gp2 maxes at 16,000 IOPS. HDDs (st1, sc1) cannot deliver the IOPS or latency needed.

questions.question: You have an 8 GB gp2 volume and expand it to 20 GB in the AWS console. After running growpart and xfs_growfs, what is still TRUE?

options.text: You can shrink it back to 8 GB
The volume size can only be increased, never decreased
You must create a new instance to use the expanded volume

explanation.correct: EBS volumes can only be expanded — you cannot reduce a volume's size. To downsize, you must create a smaller volume and copy data manually.
explanation.why: This is a critical constraint for capacity planning — always size conservatively and scale up as needed.

questions.question: Which storage option provides the HIGHEST I/O performance for a single EC2 instance but loses all data when the instance stops?

explanation.correct: Instance Store offers the highest raw I/O performance since it is physically on the host machine — but it is ephemeral. Data is lost on stop, termination, or hardware failure.
explanation.why: Instance Store is suited for temporary buffers, caches, or scratch data — never for data you need to keep.

questions.question: You delete an EC2 instance but forgot to delete its attached EBS volume. What happens?

options.text: The EBS volume is automatically deleted
The EBS volume is moved to S3
The EBS volume persists and continues to incur charges
The EBS volume is converted to a snapshot

explanation.correct: Unless the 'Delete on Termination' option was enabled, the EBS volume survives instance deletion and continues to accrue storage charges.
explanation.why: Always check for orphaned EBS volumes in your account to avoid unexpected costs.

questions.question: What is the key difference between IOPS and Throughput in the context of EBS?

options.text: IOPS measures read/write operations per second; Throughput measures data transferred per second (MB/s)
IOPS is for SSDs only; Throughput is for HDDs only
Throughput is always higher than IOPS

explanation.correct: IOPS counts the number of read/write operations per second (important for small, random I/O). Throughput measures actual data volume moved per second (important for large, sequential I/O).
explanation.why: A workload can have high IOPS but low throughput (small files) or high throughput but lower IOPS (large sequential reads).

questions.question: Which combination correctly describes EBS vs Instance Store?

options.text: EBS: ephemeral, physically attached | Instance Store: persistent, network-attached
EBS: persistent, network-attached | Instance Store: ephemeral, physically attached
Both are persistent; EBS is faster
Both are ephemeral; Instance Store is more expensive

explanation.correct: EBS is a persistent, network-attached block storage service. Instance Store is ephemeral, physically attached directly to the host machine.
explanation.why: This distinction is a frequent exam topic — EBS persists beyond instance lifecycle; Instance Store does not.
